Real time monitoring in computer integrated manufacturing | by ASHWINI MOGAL | Medium
By ASHWINI MOGAL
Real time monitoring in computer integrated manufacturing Definition of computational
monitoring in real time · Many structural, mechanical, and geotechnical systems, such as
bridges, offshore and subsurface structures, power generation systems, rotating machinery,
buildings, geotechnical foundations, boreholes, and mining excavations and tailings, and
even cases involving living matter, require continuous information about performance and
integrity of engineering systems in real time. · The absence of timely, accurate, and
consistent knowledge on manufacturing things (resources) during manufacturing execution is
currently one of the most common difficulties that manufacturing firms encounter.

Decision
makers may make better-informed shop-floor decisions with real-time information visibility
and traceability. · The internet of manufacturing things (IoMT) as a real-time information
capture and integration architecture to create a new paradigm by extending IoT principles
to the manufacturing area.

Manufacturing items such as operators, machines, pallets, and
materials, among others, may be embedded with sensors and communicate with one another
thanks to this architecture and its core components. · A Real-time Manufacturing
Information Integration Service (RTMIIS) has been designed to achieve seamless dual-way
connectivity and interoperability among the enterprise layer, workshop floor layer, and
machine layer, despite the challenges of processing a large amount of real-time data into
useful information and exchanging it among heterogeneous application systems.

Finally, a
real-world situation was used to demonstrate the suggested IoMT’s proof-of-concept
application. Motivation for computational monitoring in real time Novel materials are used
in several engineering systems.

Its long-term performance has yet to be established
Continuous monitoring of the performance of the innovative materials and improved service
time prediction are required for these systems. Transitioning to more cost-effective
technologies may also need a reduction in safety margins.

In this instance, safety
necessitates more precise monitoring. Long-term monitoring observations may be used to
update knowledge on system behaviour, which can then be incorporated through computational
modelling to improve operational performance.

Rapid condition monitoring is necessary in
extreme events to check the integrity of engineering systems and warn of impending failure
or even disaster. In this case, computational monitoring allows for speedy response to
quickly changing situations.

While the breakdown of an engineering structure or a
structure in the Earth’s crust is generally an immediate occurrence that creates a
critical point on the time axis, the processes that lead up to this critical event take
time. Naturally, the monitoring is focused on these operations, the speed of which
establishes the concept of’real time.’ We’ll suppose that these processes are defined by
their characteristic times; the process’s characteristic time is the time it takes for the
process to complete.

We also assume that the minimum typical time of the processes that
lead to the system’s failure is known, and we’ll refer to it as the system’s
characteristic time. As a result, monitoring in real time refers to a monitoring approach
whose aggregated reaction time (the time required to acquire, analyse, and present the
findings in a decision-making format) is less than the characteristic time of the system
being monitored.

Many manufacturing organisations still face the following issues 1. To
develop an overall data capture and integration architecture and solution to sense,
process, and exchange real-time manufacturing data between the enterprise layer, workshop
floor layer, and machine layer.

2. Determining how to quickly and efficiently implement
IoT technology like RFID sensors for tracking and tracing manufactured items throughout
the execution stage.

3. how to handle and integrate real-time production data in order to
accomplish smooth dual processing enterprise layer, workshop floor layer, and machine
layer communication and interoperability Components of real-time computational monitoring
Computational monitoring is an interdisciplinary approach to monitoring. a study field
that encompasses a variety of fundamental sciences, Mechanics, materials science,
electronics, and other fields Computer science is the study of computers. The most
important elements of a real-time system here are computational monitoring systems.

Evaluation and non-destructive  Processing of signal  Monitoring data analysis and
interpretations  Actuators and sensors  Computing at a high level An overall real-time
information capturing and integration architecture of the internet of manufacturing things
(IoMT) is presented to provide a new paradigm by extending the IoT to the manufacturing
field, taking into account the advantages of IoT and the requirements of real-time data
driven optimal decision of the manufacturing execution system. Manufacturing objects, such
as workers, equipment, pallets, and materials, may be integrated with sensors using this
IoMT architecture.

They can then engage with one another. As a result, the updated
information and its state may be tracked and connected with a variety of business
information systems (EISs).

The proposed IoMT attempts to bridge the gap between
enterprise management information systems and representative execution units like
workstations and trolleys. It will make real-time data-driven optimum control and
decision-making easier throughout industrial execution.

The Internet of Things (IoT) and
its applications in the industrial industry The Auto-ID centre popularised the Internet of
Things concept. There have been a variety of definitions for the Internet of Things. According to Casagras (http://www.rfidglobal.eu/userfiles/documents/CASAGRAS26022009.pdf),
the Internet of Things (IoT) is a global network architecture that connects physical and
virtual items using data capture and communication capabilities.

Existing and emerging
Internet and network advancements are included in this infrastructure. IoT is an
integrated part of the Future Internet, according to CERP-IoT (Antoine de 2009), and can
be defined as a dynamic global network infrastructure with self-configuring capabilities
based on standard and interoperable communication protocols, where physical and virtual
‘things’ have identities, physical attributes, and virtual attributes.

Processing and
integration of manufacturing data When information is shared among heterogeneous
application systems in real-life manufacturing organisations, difficulties in information
integration may develop due to the many software applications employed in different
enterprises. As a result, manufacturing information standard models and schemas play a
significant role in information exchange and integration across diverse corporate systems.

Siemens Energy & Automation, Inc. (2006) has created an interface that allows enterprise
resource planning (ERP) and process control systems to communicate seamlessly. The
challenges, trends, and difficulties for enterprise information interoperability are
described by Panetto and Molin (2008).

They claim that enterprise knowledge sharing,
shared best practises, and open source/web-based applications make it possible to
accomplish the idea of integrated enterprise, and hence networked enterprise
implementation and interoperability. The ISA95 standard (ANSI/ISA 2000) was created with
the goal of lowering the cost, risk, and mistakes involved with integrating enterprise and
production control systems.

The World Batch Forum (WBF) produced the business-to-
manufacturing markup language (B2MML 2003) standard, which provides approved concepts and
data. forms for exchanging information across management systems Anaya et al.

(2010)
present a unified model. UEML (Enterprise Modeling Language) is a language for modelling
businesses.

facilitating the usage of corporate information models represented in a
variety of languages. To execute the information integration of heterogeneous information
s0ystems, Zhang, Huang, and Qu (2011) use XML (extensible markup language) based schemas.

For shop-floor work-in-progress (WIP) management, Fang, Huang, and Li (2013) describe an
event-driven multi-agent ubiquitous manufacturing execution platform. Current industrial
data integration models and methods, on the other hand, are primarily focused on
heterogeneous corporate data systems.

Because the crucial real-time data in IoMT
originates straight from the basic events of Auto-ID devices, how do you develop a
manufacturing information processing and integration approach that works across the
enterprise layer, workshop floor layer, and cloud layer? However, the overall integration
architecture, real-time manufacturing data processing solution, and exchange standard
among enterprise layer, workshop floor layer, and machine layer should be further designed
based on the IoT infrastructure to make real-time production monitoring and control of the
entire enterprise easy to deploy and use.

Furthermore, the manufacturing information
integration described above is already being utilised to deal with information sharing
among third-party EISs; however, little thought has been given to how to seamlessly
integrate and share real-time and multisource manufacturing data with third-party EISs. As
a result, this study proposes and designs an overall real-time information capture and
integration architecture for IoMT to solve the new problems.

IoMT’s overall architecture
With improved planning, scheduling, and control decisions, real-time traceability and
visibility of manufacturing items plays a crucial role in increasing shop-floor
performance. The goal of this study is to adapt the IoT idea to the manufacturing area and
create a referenced real-time data collection and integration architecture for
manufacturing companies.

By referring to IoT infrastructure, an overall real-time data
capturing and analysis. Real-time tracking and tracing of each manufacturing object
(resource) is possible with this architecture.

The entire production execution process may
then be observed in real time. Sensor networks are used to monitor dynamical
characteristics such as the environment (temperature, pressure, humidity, and so on),
movement (velocity, acceleration, shock, and so on), and the real-time state of
manufactured objects.

It will give supervisors real-time data to execute optimal control
and decision-making in a production execution system. From the bottom to the top, the
proposed IoMT consists of four components: configuration of smart manufacturing items,
primitive event detection and capturing, manufacturing data processing, and application
services.

Smart manufacturing object configuration Smart manufacturing item configuration
is responsible for increasing the sensing capabilities of all types of manufacturing
objects (resources). The physical manufacturing resources are equipped with Auto-ID
devices to reach a specific level of intelligence, which makes smart manufacturing things
“smart.” In this IoMT framework, auto-ID techniques like RFID will be used to
manufacturing resources like machines and production lines to create smart manufacturing
objects that can detect the real-time state of manufacturing things including operators,
materials, locations, and WIP items.

Sensing and recording of primitive events The real-
time primitive event of the sensors fitted to the manufacturing resources may be sensed
and collected throughout the production process based on the setup of the smart
manufacturing devices. A general technique is shown in Figure 2.

The basic event can be
perceived by the registered sensor when a manufactured object approaches a sensing region. The sensor can gather and transfer data from incoming manufacturing objects to the IoMT
using the communication protocol and relationships in the registry.

An RFID reader
situated at a machine, for example, may detect and collect the electronic product code
(EPC) of an operator wearing an RFID tag. Data processing in manufacturing A large
quantity of real-time data collected by Auto-ID devices cannot be used directly in higher-
level EISs.

The data processing component in manufacturing is utilised to process the
insignificant data into meaningful manufacturing information. Figure 3 illustrates a
simple example of data processing.

Take RFID technologies as an example: in sensing and
capturing stage, the EPC of each tag attached to the manufacturing things is sensed and
captured. However, this captured data is of no use for manufacturing system.

Data
processing is responsible for establishing the mapping relation and mechanism. Conclusion
We’ve built the fundamentals for real-time computational monitoring.

The computational
monitoring has been defined.as a hybrid monitoring strategy that combines continuous
measurement with real-time interpretation and forecasting Computational monitoring, in our
opinion, is the next stage in the creation of intelligent engineering systems that can
monitor their operating conditions, foresee faults, and govern their performance. We’ve
shown that standard monitoring approaches in several sectors of engineering share basic
characteristics and face similar obstacles when it comes to incorporating data from
various sources measurement.

We also looked at the measurement methodologies and
computational models that may be used to monitor diverse engineering systems in real time. The examination is brought to a close with examples from geotechnical engineering.

We
anticipate that this study will spark discussion and cross-fertilization between
monitoring approaches being developed in many fields of engineering, assisting in the
resolution of computational monitoring difficulties, some of which are listed below. · The
essential features of the monitored system, such as stiffness, energy dissipation, and so
on, are altered when damage accumulates.

The challenge is to guarantee that the
interpretation models are constantly and often adjusted in real time to adapt to system
changes. This is especially significant for data collecting based on vibration, acoustic
emission, and electromagnetic emission with model-based analysis.

 A key difficulty for
computational monitoring systems is the design of the needed measurement system and sensor
networks prior to deployment.The interpretation models must be able to react to changes in
the measurement system, such as sensor failures at random.  Another problem is the
creation of correlation models between signal-based and model-based interpretation
approaches.

These models are required to guarantee that effective monitoring processes are
in place.
